He would not be able to reliably profit off of the fact that the market has priced in this risk, unless the market was consistently wrong in forecasting bankruptcy. Have I understood this correctly? text:
Is there any downside to using tax-deferred account with the intent of terminating before maturity?

Imagine someone subject to taxation by the federal republic of germany ( unbeschränkt steuerpflichtig ) and planning to invest over a 20-year horizon. On a typical account used for buying and holding low-risk investment fund shares that person will use money that is already (income) taxed, and owe capital gains tax ( Kapitalertragssteuer ) upon every realization of profits, some of which will need to be paid in advance ( Vorabpauschale ), thereby limiting compound interest. On an account with otherwise matching composition over time but held under a contract qualified under the the new § 1 section (1b) AltZertG ( Altersvorsorgedepot-Vertrag ) it appears as if that person has the option of deferring taxes, up to the age of 70: Until that age they could terminate the contract early ( § 93 Schädliche Verwendung ) and pay taxes on the lump sum. Which could realistically secure a huge advantage from compound interest, and even retain interest accrued from bonuses that were returned on cancellation. That is not how these retirement-oriented contracts are meant to be used - one is expected to receive regular payouts starting at some age between typically 65 or 70 - yet I do not see what would deter people from using them for other investing, with intent to cancel early from the outset. The latter option sounds too much like a bargain, at the expense of federal budget. Where is the catch? Reading related posts on the US "traditional IRA" type of account that seems to have served as an ideological template for the new German scheme, one would expect the catch to be a substantial tax disadvantage upon cancelling early. However, I have found no such disadvantage in the (sparse) information available so far. (At the time of writing the question nobody can know the answer from having tried. There may be relevant differences from the existing section (1) contracts, and no section (1b) contract can possibly exist yet; certification is set to begin no earlier than 2027-01-01.)

Two US taxpayers, A and B, own a home together as joint tenants.  They both live in the home, and it is their "main home" for tax purposes.  A and B are not married to each other and never have been, and they each file their taxes as "single". There is a mortgage on the home, in the name of A and B jointly, and they each meet the criteria to take the home mortgage interest deduction .  They each pay half of the monthly mortgage payments. For example, suppose that in a given year, the mortgage payments totaled $40,000, of which $10,000 was principal and $30,000 was interest.  A and B each paid $20,000. By default, each of them would say they paid $5,000 in principal and $15,000 in interest, and each would take a $15,000 mortgage interest deduction.  But could they instead say that the $20,000 paid by A was entirely interest, and that B paid the entire $10,000 in principal plus the remaining $10,000 in interest?  That would result in A taking a $20,000 deduction, and B taking a $10,000 deduction.  This might be advantageous if A is in a higher tax bracket, or if A itemizes and B does not. Pub. 936 (linked above) has a section "More than one borrower": More than one borrower. If you and at least one other person (other than your spouse if you file a joint return) were liable for and paid interest on a mortgage that was for your home, and the other person received a Form 1098 showing the interest that was paid during the year, attach a statement to your paper return explaining this. Show how much of the interest each of you paid, and give the name and address of the person who received the form. I checked a few of the websites where ETF providers document their respective funds. If I want to know what some iShares or Xtrackers fund is actually holding I can just download some predictably structured URL . Easy.
Try the same thing with (afaict, also regarded reputable) Amundi .. need to manually click through a one or more pointless prompts. Then not even a download URL on the fund website , just a bunch of scripted mess that sometimes manages to correctly convert the displayed graph data into a downloadable Microsoft file format. Its like the Vanguard site, but more broken. But at least every time the the file does download, it contains the data. Next up I checked UBS . Or might have, if I had the patience. They even put some salt in the wound by openly admitting that they know good and well that their website was not made to work reliably: Please wait for the requested content to load. If there is no response after several minutes, please reload the page or try again later. Next up, I tried Invesco .. I have yet to find proof they even have a CSV download link somewhere (on the US page there is one). It gets worse from there. Most seem to begrudgingly publish legally required information .. but then spent significant extra effort to make it extra annoying for anyone actually bothering to access. Someone doing this for a living could probably automate away the friction, so it only disadvantages individual investors. And since I found the counter-examples above that do not play games, there cannot be any strict necessity behind it. Is there anything nefarious (or at least deliberate information asymmetry) going on here, or is it just a case of bad websites being bad? EDIT: I suspect that what they are doing is considered in compliance with directive 2009/65/EC. If the existing publication obligations already came with enforceable "accessible" + "up-to-date" requirements, then the 2028 changes adding ESAP requirements would not need to spell out "data extractable format" . Sounds to me like lawmakers adding this because before that change, publishing half-yearly reports sufficed.

text:
Are UK pension overpayments recoverable where the pension scheme itself calculated and confirmed the amount?

I am trying to understand how UK law treats pension overpayments where the recipient had no obvious way of knowing they were being overpaid. In a recent question here the questioner asks about repaying a dividend that is accidentally paid twice. In this instance, it seems clear that the recipient of the mistaken payment is aware of the mistaken payment and should repay it. Section 5(4) of The Theft Act 1968 was quoted in an answer to that question: Where a person gets property by another’s mistake, and is under an obligation to make restoration ... an intention not to make restoration shall be regarded accordingly as an intention to deprive that person of the property or proceeds. But pensions seem different. The pension scheme or administrator is the body that calculates and states the member’s entitlement. If a person receives pension payments for years, has no reason to know the amount is wrong, and perhaps even queries the amount and is told it is correct, then they may make retirement and spending decisions on that basis. A recent Guardian article reports that civil service, NHS and Post Office pensioners being asked to repay large historic overpayments caused by administrative errors, including one case where the pensioner had queried the figures and been reassured they were correct. The Pensions Ombudsman also says that pension overpayments are usually recoverable, but that members may have legal defences depending on the facts. My question is: In England and Wales, when a UK occupational or public-sector pension scheme overpays a member for years due to its own calculation or administrative error, what legal principles determine whether the member must repay the historic overpayment? It seems particularly unfair, because at this point in their lives people set their lifestyle and habits based on their income. So even just having one's income set to the correct level after having been receiving the (incorrect) higher amount is going to be difficult. Then having to repay the debt out of this reduced income is going to reduce the standard of living even more. Whereas it seems that if I as an individual make a financial mistake - e.g. I sell my car for £5,000 and realise after it's sold that it was actually worth £15,000 (maybe because it has become a sought-after vintage car) - I can't go back to the buyer and ask for more money. I guess some things that might feed into this would be: Does the scheme’s negligence or delay prevent recovery, or is the starting point still that the member was only ever entitled to the correct pension under the scheme rules? How do defences such as “change of position”, hardship, or maladministration apply? Is there a difference between correcting future pension payments and recovering past overpayments? Does it matter if the member specifically queried the pension amount and received written or verbal confirmation that it was correct? Are there special rules for public-sector schemes, where the administrator may say it has a duty to recover public money? I am not asking for advice on a specific case, but for the general legal/financial principles and how they differ from an obvious mistaken duplicate payment.
label: regulation

text:
Does this substack article on "the illusion of diversification" make sense?

This posting on substack uses much terminology about dot products and wedge products that will not be understood by most non-mathematicians, but the idea is something like this: Suppose two stocks usually either rise or fall together, or if one of them usually rises when the other falls, or if 3 times the price of the first stock minus 4 times the price of the second stock plus 2 times the price of the third stock typically rises when the fourth stock rises, etc., etc., then you have less diversity than if all the stocks behaved independently of each other. That part seems clear enough. The simplest and most extreme case of this is an investor whose portfolio is two shares of one company, but he thinks they are shares of two different companies. Clearly he has less diversity than if they were shares of two unrelated companies. The author goes on to say that if "your assets are linearly dependent," then "They are trapped on a 2D plane. You are infinitely exposed to any risk factor perpendicular to that plane. You have Phantom Diversification." Understanding that requires a bit of math, but in that "simplest and most extreme case" mentioned above the "plane" in which you are "trapped" is that in which the two stock prices will always be equal, and the "risk factor perpendicular to that plane" is the price of the first stock minus the price of the second stock. This ignorant investor does not know that the price of the first stock minus the price of the second will never fluctuate and will always remain zero. It seems to me that if he is thus "infinitely exposed" to some "risk factor", it must be because of his ignorance of the fact that the two shares he owns are both of the same company. So my question is this: How would someone take advantage of his ignorance of that fact by buying something from him or selling something to him, in a way that would not be possible if he knew that his two shares were both of the same company?

text:
Nonresident alien with U.S.-source §988 gain: ECI, FDAP, or not taxable?

Facts •   Taxpayer is a nonresident alien who does not meet the substantial presence test but lives and works in the U.S. •   After moving to the U.S. and establishing a U.S. tax home through employment, the taxpayer converts foreign personal savings (e.g., EUR) to USD. •   The foreign currency represents personal savings accumulated over multiple prior years; upon conversion, the USD amount realized exceeds the taxpayer’s basis determined under §988 due solely to exchange-rate movements. •   The resulting foreign currency gain is ordinary income under §988. Sourcing Under §865, foreign currency gain is sourced by the taxpayer’s residence, and residence is determined by tax home under §911(d)(3).
Because the taxpayer’s principal place of business is in the U.S., the §988 gain appears to be U.S.-source income. Issue: How is this §988 gain taxed to a nonresident alien? Analysis •   The gain does not appear to be effectively connected income (ECI): it arises from personal savings and is not connected to a U.S. trade or business; the taxpayer’s U.S. employment is not a material factor in producing the gain. •   The gain also does not appear to be FDAP income: Under Reg. §1.988-3(c)(1), exchange gain or loss on a §988  transaction is not treated as interest, except in limited, specifically enumerated cases (e.g., certain tax-exempt bonds, integrated debt hedges). The §988 regulations treat the conversion of nonfunctional currency as a sale or other disposition of property, applying §1001 amount-realized and basis mechanics. Gains from sales or other dispositions of property are excluded from FDAP under Reg. §1.1441-2(b)(2)(i). Question If the gain is U.S.-source but is neither ECI nor FDAP, is it correct that the §988 gain is not taxable to the nonresident alien under §871, notwithstanding its ordinary character?

text:
Why isn't the "erase and replace" strategy routine for avoiding estimated payments and delaying taxes (for married retirees with IRAs, at least)?

Assume that a retired, married U.S. couple receives capital gains, possibly erratic, throughout the year for whatever reason. The prevailing recommendation is to complete IRS Form 2210 Schedule AI throughout the year* to calculate estimated tax payments and to make these payments in a timely manner to avoid penalties. The (sometimes needless**) payments represent money that's no longer available to earn income. As an alternative, consider the "erase and replace" approach, in which withholding from an IRA rollover is used to satisfy the required payments. ( 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 .) (The IRS considers withholding at any point in the year to be distributed evenly over the four payment periods.) In this strategy, the couple makes zero estimated payments throughout the year and then performs an indirect IRA rollover each December in the amount of 90% of that year's tax or 100-110% of last year's tax (depending on their AGI), whichever is less. It's arranged that 100% of the rollover is withheld for federal taxes; the rollover is completed soon after with cash. An indirect rollover is permitted every 12 months per person; to avoid having the date creep forward when meeting this requirement, the couple alternates between rollovers for each person, resulting in ~24 months spacing. Thus, Federal tax is considered to be paid in a timely manner, No penalties are incurred, Form 2210 can potentially be ignored, and Instead of making estimated payments (which may be refunded anyway, as described below), that money can be used to earn income starting as early as April 15 (the deadline for the first estimated payment) to the rollover replacement date (as @littleadv indicates, this minimizes the amount of time the rollover money is absent from the IRA). Note that this strategy addresses federal tax only; state laws vary regarding withholding and estimated payments. I see no indication that this approach is recommended for routine use, so either there's an error or it's an obscure edge case (although it doesn't seem unusual for a retired couple to both have IRAs and also receive capital gains). I appreciate your comments. *Example of a "gotcha" if the couple doesn't complete Form 2210 Schedule AI throughout the year: The couple receives capital gains of $125K in January and then unexpected capital gains of $125K more in December. They spend most of the year paying zero estimated taxes, as their January income is tax free under the standard deduction and 0% capital gains bracket. In December, when they turn out to owe tax on $250K capital gains for the year, Schedule AI reveals retrospectively that the required first-period estimated payment is the lesser of 1/4 of 90% of this year's tax, or 1/4 of 100-110% of last year's tax (depending on their AGI), or 22% of the tax on first-period-annualized 4 × $125K = $500K (Schedule AI, part I, lines 1-21). None of these numbers is zero, and so a penalty is incurred. (Discussed in this answer , described as the "gold standard" on the topic, and in this answer and this one .) **Example of a needless payment: Wary of the "gotcha" described above, the couple makes an estimated payment in the first period. If no more capital gains are received after January, however, the federal tax ends up being zero after all, and that payment is refunded in full in the following year, representing a loss in potential investment income.
